en: The *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra*. Homage to the glorious Mañjughoṣa!
The Blessed One said: "And what, monks, is this Dharma-discourse called the *Arthaviniścaya*?"
As it has been said: the five aggregates (skandhas),
the five aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandhas),
and the eighteen elements (dhātus).
The twelve sense bases;
dependent origination with its twelve factors;
the four noble truths.
The twenty-two faculties;
the four meditative absorptions; [the four formless attainments].
The four divine abodes;
the four analytical knowledges;
the four cultivations of meditative concentration.
The four foundations of mindfulness;
the four right efforts;
the four bases of psychic power.
The five faculties,
the five powers,
and the seven factors of enlightenment.
The noble eightfold path;
the sixteen aspects of mindfulness of breathing;
the four factors of stream-entry.
The ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges,
and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The thirty-two marks of a great person and the eighty secondary characteristics. This, monks, is the summary of the Dharma discourse entitled "The Determination of Meaning."

(1) In this regard, monks, what are the five aggregates? They are as follows: the aggregate of form; the aggregate of feeling; [the aggregate of perception; the aggregate of mental formations; and the aggregate of consciousness].
The aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
Monks, these are the five aggregates.

(2) In this regard, monks, what are the five aggregates of clinging? They are as follows: the aggregate of clinging to form; the aggregate of clinging to feeling; [the aggregate of clinging to perception; the aggregate of clinging to mental formations; and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness].
The aggregate of clinging to perception; the aggregate of clinging to mental formations; the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
Monks, these are the five aggregates of clinging.
(3) In this regard, monks, what are the eighteen elements? They are as follows: the eye element; the form element; [and so forth].
The element of eye-consciousness;
the element of the ear; the element of sound.
The element of auditory consciousness.
The nose element,
the odor element,
and the nose-consciousness element.
The tongue element; the taste element;
the tongue-consciousness element.
The body element,
the tangibility element,
and the body-consciousness element.
The mind element,
the mental-object element,
and the mind-consciousness element.
Monks, these are called the eighteen elements.
(4) In this regard, monks, what are the twelve sense bases?
Namely: the internal sense base of the eye;
the internal sense base of form.
The ear is the internal sense base;
sound is the external sense base;
the nose is the internal sense base.
Odor is the external sense base;
the tongue is the internal sense base;
taste is the external sense base.
The body is the internal sense base;
contact is the external sense base;
the mind is the internal sense base.
Dharma is the external sense-base.
These, monks, are called the twelve sense-bases.
(5) In this regard, monks, what is dependent origination with its twelve factors?
Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces;
conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness.
Conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form;
conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases;
conditioned by the six sense bases is contact.
Conditioned by contact is feeling;
conditioned by feeling is craving;
conditioned by craving is grasping.
With clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises;
and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness;
from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form.
From the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases;
from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact;
from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling.
From the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving;
from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence.
From the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
from the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
(a) In this regard, what is ignorance?
It is that which is non-knowledge concerning the past and non-knowledge concerning the future.
Ignorance regarding the past; ignorance regarding the future; ignorance regarding the internal; ignorance regarding the external.
Ignorance regarding the internal and external; ignorance regarding karma; ignorance regarding its maturation.
Ignorance regarding the ripening of karma; ignorance regarding wholesome action;
ignorance regarding unwholesome action.
Ignorance regarding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena;
ignorance regarding the cause; ignorance regarding the fruit.
Ignorance regarding cause and fruit;
ignorance regarding phenomena arisen from causes; ignorance regarding dependent origination.
Ignorance regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently; ignorance regarding the Buddha;
ignorance regarding the Dharma.
Ignorance regarding the Saṅgha; ignorance regarding suffering; ignorance regarding the origin [of suffering].
Ignorance regarding cessation; ignorance regarding the path; ignorance regarding the wholesome.
Ignorance regarding the unwholesome;
ignorance regarding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena;
ignorance regarding that which is blameworthy.
Ignorance regarding what is blameless;
ignorance regarding dharmas that are blameworthy or blameless; and ignorance regarding what is to be cultivated.
Ignorance regarding what is not to be cultivated;
ignorance regarding those dharmas that are to be cultivated and those that are not to be cultivated;
and ignorance regarding that which is associated with outflows (sāsrava).
Ignorance regarding the untainted;
ignorance regarding tainted and untainted phenomena;
ignorance regarding the conditioned.
Ignorance regarding the unconditioned;
ignorance regarding conditioned and unconditioned phenomena;
ignorance regarding the past.
Ignorance regarding the future; ignorance regarding the present;
ignorance regarding phenomena of the past, future, and present.
Ignorance regarding the six bases of contact— lack of knowledge, lack of vision, lack of clear realization, darkness, delusion, and the gloom of nescience— this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
(ā) "Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces.
What are the formative forces?
There are three types of formative forces: the bodily formative force, the vocal formative force, and the mental formative force.
In that regard, what is the bodily formation? It is inhalation and exhalation,
for this is a physical phenomenon.
It is dependent on the body and bound to the body;
it exists in reliance upon the body.
Therefore, inhalation and exhalation are called "bodily formations" (*kāyasaṃskāra*).
What is the formative factor of speech?
Having applied thought and sustained thought, one utters speech; not without having applied thought, nor without having sustained thought.
Therefore, initial inquiry and sustained investigation are called the formative forces of speech.
What is the mental formation? It is the volition of one who is impassioned,
and that of the mind.
Therefore, his volition is a mental factor (caitasika),
for it is dependent upon the mind and bound to the mind.
It proceeds depending upon the mind;
therefore, volition is called a mental formation.
(i) "Consciousness has formations as its condition.
What is consciousness?
It is the six groups of consciousness.
Which six? Namely: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and nose-consciousness.
Tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
These are the six groups of consciousness.
(ī) "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises].
In this context, "name-and-form": "name" refers to the four formless aggregates.
Which four?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.
The aggregate of consciousness.
This is name.
What is form?
Whatever is form,
that consists of the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements.
Namely: the earth element,
the water element,
and the fire element.
The wind element.
What is the earth element? That which is heaviness and hardness.
What is the water element?
That which is fluidity and the state of flowing.
What is the fire element?
That which is heat and the state of ripening.
What is the wind element? It is that which is contraction, expansion, and lightness-and-motion.
This is the [nature of] form as previously described.
These two, when condensed together into one, are called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
(u) "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases [arise]. What are the six sense bases? The eye base, and so forth.
The sense base of the ear; the sense base of the nose; the sense base of the tongue.
The sense-base of the body; the sense-base of the mind.
This is called the six sense-bases.
(ū) "With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact.
What is contact?
It is the six groups of contact: eye-contact, [ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact].
Auditory contact; olfactory contact; gustatory contact.
Body-contact; mind-contact.
(This is called contact.)
(e) Feeling has contact as its condition.
What is feeling? It consists of the six types of feeling.
Which six?
Feeling born of eye-contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
feeling born of ear-contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Feeling born of nose-contact is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
feeling born of tongue-contact is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
feeling born of body-contact is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Feeling born of mental contact is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
this is called feeling.
(o) Craving has feeling as its condition.
What is craving?
It consists of the six classes of craving.
Which six? Craving for forms, craving for sounds, and craving for odors.
Craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
(This is called craving.)
(ka) Craving is the condition for clinging. What is clinging?
There are four kinds of clinging.
Which four? Clinging to craving;
clinging to rules and observances.
The grasping of self-awareness—
this is called grasping.
(kha) "With grasping as condition, there is existence.
What is existence? There are three types of existence.
Which three?
Existence in the realm of desire; existence in the realm of form.
And there is the formless existence (*ārūpyabhava*).
Among these, what is sensual existence (*kāmabhava*)?
It is as follows: the hells.
Animals, hungry ghosts,
asuras,
and the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm.
They are as follows: the eight great hells.
Which are the eight? They are as follows: the hot great hells.
Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, and Saṃghāta.
And two Rauravas;
Tapana; Pratāpana.
And Avīci.
Thus.
The great hells.
Namely: Arbuda,
Nirarbuda,
and Aṭaṭa.
Hahavaḥ | Huhuvaḥ | Utpalaḥ |
Padma; Mahāpadma.
Which are the six classes of gods? The gods of the Four Great Kings; the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
The Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, and the Nirmāṇarati gods.
The gods who wield power over the creations of others.
In that regard, what is existence in the realm of form? It is as follows: the gods of the Brahma-realm (Brahmakāyika) and the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita).
The Mahābrahmās; the Parīttābhas; the Apramāṇābhas.
The Ābhāsvara [deities], the Parīttashubha [deities], and the Apramāṇashubha [deities].
The Śubhakṛtsnas, the Anabhrakas, and the Puṇyaprasavas.
The Abṛha heavens; the Atapa heavens; the Abṛha heavens.
The Sudarśanas and the Akaniṣṭhas.
What are the formless realms? They are as follows: the sphere of infinite space;
the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The sphere of nothingness;
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
For the formless gods and for those who meditate on mind-only, there are four modes of rebirth;
this is called "existence conditioned by grasping."
(ga) "Birth has existence as its condition.
What is birth? It is the birth of those various sentient beings within their respective classes of beings.
Birth, descent [into the womb], and manifestation.
The manifestation of the aggregates, the acquisition of the sense bases, and the arising of the life-faculty.
(This is called birth.)
(g) (With birth as condition, there is aging and death.
What is aging?

It is that which, within the continuity of one's homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāgatā*), consists of baldness, graying of hair, abundance of wrinkles, decrepitude, stooping, crookedness like a rafter, labored inhalation and exhalation, and a body marred by freckles and age spots.

The forward-leaning of the body, the need for support by a staff, the maturation and disintegration of the sense faculties, the state of being worn out and decrepit, the slowness, dullness, decline, and loss— this is called old age.
In that regard, what is death?

It is the falling away of those beings from that physical body; it is passing away, dissolution, disappearance, death, the completion of one's time, the loss of vitality, the loss of heat, the cessation of the life-faculty, and the casting off of the aggregates.
This is called death.
This death together with the aforementioned aging— when these two are condensed into one— is called "aging-and-death."
Monks, this is the analysis of this twelvefold dependent origination.
(6) In that regard, what are the four noble truths? They are as follows: the noble truth of suffering; the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
The noble truth of the cessation of suffering;
the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of suffering? It is as follows: birth is suffering;
aging is suffering.
Sickness is suffering;
death is suffering;
separation from the beloved is suffering.
Association with the unpleasant is suffering;
form is suffering;
feeling is suffering.
Perception is suffering; mental formations are suffering; consciousness is suffering.
Furthermore, that which is not found even when sought in this manner is also suffering.
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; this is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

It is the complete abandonment, relinquishment, exhaustion, destruction, fading away, and cessation of this very craving—which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there; this is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is the noble eightfold path, beginning with right view.

For example, suppose a certain man, overcome by fever, approaches a physician who is accomplished in skill, has witnessed [the effects of] medical practice, and is learned in the scriptures, and says this: "I am not at peace due to this fever;
I desire that a medicine be prescribed for its subsiding.
That physician would first ask him about the cause: "What have you eaten and what have you drunk?"
The patient would say to him, "I have indeed eaten curd and cucumber; I have drunk food, drink, and buttermilk.
The physician, having instructed him on the specific [dietary restrictions], would then prescribe the medicine.

In the very same way, virtuous persons tormented by the great fever of birth and so forth approach the Tathāgata—the Great Physician, the Lord of Great Compassion—and inquire about the Dharma that removes the fever of suffering.
To them, the Blessed One explains its origin and its arising, and teaches the Noble Eightfold Path as the great medicine that brings peace and leads to Nirvāṇa.
Even one afflicted by the defilements, by cultivating this path, will before long attain the destruction of all suffering; having gone to the city of Nirvāṇa, they obtain complete tranquility.
These indeed, monks, are the four noble truths.
(7) In this regard, monks, what is the noble eightfold path? It is as follows: right view and right intention.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Right effort,
right mindfulness,
and right concentration.
In this regard, monks, what is right view?
There is this world; there is a world beyond.
There is a father;
there is what is given; there is what is offered in sacrifice.

"There is the ripening of the fruits of actions that are desirable and undesirable, well-done and ill-done; there are in the world those who have attained the right path and who have practiced rightly.
Monks, this is right view.
What is right resolve? It is generosity dedicated toward [the attainment of] Buddhahood and so forth, and ethical discipline dedicated toward [the status of] a universal monarch and so forth.
This, monks, is right intention.
What is right speech? Here, monks, it is speech that avoids harshness, falsehood, slander, and frivolous chatter; it is truthful speech.
This is called right speech.
What is right action?
It is the engagement of body, speech, and mind in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Among these, bodily action is threefold: abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct.
Vocal [action] is fourfold: abstaining from false speech, harsh speech, slanderous speech, and frivolous chatter. Mental [action] is threefold: abstaining from covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
In that regard, what is the taking of life? It is when there is a living being,
and one perceives it as a living being.
And one gives rise to a murderous intent and deprives [the being] of life;
this, monks, is called the taking of life.
Except in cases of negligence or through lack of perception, there is no taking of life.
In that regard, what is taking what is not given?
Taking possession of another's property with a thieving mind is taking what is not given;
however, the taking of a small amount of property belonging to one's mother, father, brother, kinsman, or friend, provided it does not cause them distress, is not taking what is not given.
In that regard, what is sexual misconduct?
It is the enjoyment of the wives of others— those protected by a husband, a king, a father-in-law, or parents.
Alternatively, physical misconduct consists of engaging in wrong behavior at improper places, with respect to improper objects, or at improper times;
thus it is threefold.
What is falsehood? In response to a question as a witness, to speak untruthfully or falsely, or to claim "I am an Arhat" when it is not the case—
this is called falsehood.
What is divisive speech? Divisive speech is speech that causes division, whether by means of what is untrue or what is true.

What is harsh speech? It is the act of making someone hear abusive words with the intention: "May he experience the suffering of hearing unpleasant speech," on the part of one who desires to cause suffering to another.
That is harsh speech.
What is frivolous chatter?
Talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of gambling, talk of intoxicants, talk of women, and talk of legends.
This is called frivolous chatter.
And that which is vocal is of four kinds.
What is covetousness?
It is the desire to appropriate the property of another, thinking, "May these possessions of another belong to me"; this is called covetousness.
What is ill-will? It is the thought of depriving another of life, or of cutting, harming, and so forth. This is called ill-will.
What is wrong view?
It is as stated previously: "There is no this world, there is no other world," and so forth.
This threefold mental [action] is called wrong view.
Now, what is right livelihood (*samyagājīva*)?

For a monk, right livelihood consists in the absence of hypocrisy (*kuhanā*), flattery (*lapanā*), hinting (*naimittikatva*), coercion (*naiṣpeṣikatva*), and the seeking of gain through gain (*lābhena lābhapratikāṅkṣā*).
[These are] hypocrisy, flattery, and so forth.
In that regard, what is hypocrisy (*kuhanā*)?

When a monk, upon seeing a donor, sits cross-legged on the road or in an empty house as if meditating, thinking, "I shall receive gain and honor as a monk who is an Arhat"— this and similar acts are called hypocrisy.
In that regard, what is flattery? Here, a monk, for the sake of gain and honor alone, says: "You are my mother;
you are my daughter."
In this way, he speaks other pleasing words as well;
such speech is called "flattery."

In that regard, what is "hinting" (*naimittikatva*)? It is when a monk, having consumed his alms-food, says either once or repeatedly: "Such as this alms-food is, the like of it is not obtained in the houses of other lay devotees."
However, for one who speaks with a mind free from desire for gain and honor, there is no fault at all;
this is called "hinting" (*naimittikatva*).
In that regard, what is "importunity"? It is when a monk, having failed to receive almsfood at a certain house,
desires to have it given to him.
In this regard, he says: "Those who are not masters of giving go to hell;
you too are not masters of giving, so you clearly belong among those going to hell.
Thus, to those terrified by the fear of hell, he offers alms-food.
Having obtained it, he consumes it;
this is called "being free from hypocrisy."
In that regard, what is the expectation of gain for the sake of gain?

A monk first uses his own wealth to purchase fine robes and shows them to lay followers, saying, "We obtain such garments from our benefactors. They, being thus enticed, offer him those very garments.
He consumes them;
this, monks, is called a monk’s longing for gain through gain. This, monks, is wrong livelihood.
Therefore, abstention from such [wrong livelihood] is right livelihood.
In this regard, monks, what is wrong livelihood for a lay follower? It is the sale of poison;
it is the sale of weapons.
The sale of living beings;
the sale of intoxicants;
the sale of meat.
Pressing sesame or mustard seeds without having first inspected them is a wrong livelihood for a lay follower (*upāsaka*). Abstinence from this is [the precept].
This, monks, is called right livelihood.
What is right effort?
It is frequent salutation, rising to greet others, joining the palms in reverence, and performing acts of proper courtesy.
This, monks, is called right effort.
What is right mindfulness?

Here, monks, when a monk sees a woman and lust arises, he becomes one who sees things as they truly are by way of the impure aspect of both the external and internal bodies: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, dirt, filth, skin, and flesh."

It is filled with bones, sinews, veins, kidneys, the heart, the stomach, the receptacle for undigested food (*āmāśaya*), the receptacle for digested food (*pakkāśaya*), the intestines, the mesentery, the spleen, the liver, the gallbladder, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, fat, lymph, marrow, adipose tissue, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, and brain matter; it is full of excrement and urine— impurity of many kinds.
This, monks, is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration?
It is the four dhyānas.

Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
He dwells;

with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with joy and bliss.
Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
He experiences happiness with the body— that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous"— and thus enters and dwells in the third dhyāna.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Monks, these indeed are the four dhyānas;
this is called right concentration.
This, monks, is called the noble eightfold path.
(8) What are the twenty-two faculties? Namely:

the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the male faculty, the female faculty, the faculty of suffering, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, and the life faculty.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
Monks, these are the twenty-two faculties.

(9) In this regard, monks, what are the four dhyānas? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal clarity and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by joy and bliss.
Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly conscious.
He experiences pleasure with the body— of which the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in equanimity, mindful, and at ease"— and thus enters and abides in the third dhyāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and dejection, he enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Monks, these are the four meditative absorptions.
(10) In this regard, what are the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*)?

Here, monks, a monk dwells having attained the mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from affliction, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated; having released it in all directions, pervaded it, and fully realized it, he dwells therein.
Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, throughout this entire world, he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness— free from enmity, free from ill will, unafflicted, vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, well-cultivated— and having attained it, he remains there. Likewise with a mind accompanied by compassion.

With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy, accompanied by equanimity— free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from affliction, vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, well-cultivated— he, having resolved upon one direction, pervades it, attains it, and dwells therein.
These are the four divine abodes.
(11) In that regard, what are the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)? There is a difficult practice with slow direct knowledge; there is a difficult practice with swift direct knowledge.
There is the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge;
there is the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. In that regard, what is that painful practice with slow direct knowledge?
In this case, a certain person is by nature intensely passionate, intensely hateful, and intensely deluded.
He repeatedly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of intense passion; he repeatedly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of hatred due to his intense hatred;
he repeatedly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of delusion due to his intense delusion.
For him, these five supramundane faculties are sluggish, weak, and slow-moving.
Which five?
Namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

Because these five supramundane faculties are weak and do not proceed swiftly, one touches the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*) only slowly—that is, for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*). This is the painful practice with slow superknowledge (*duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā*). In that regard, what is the painful practice with quick superknowledge?
In this case, a certain person is by nature intensely passionate, intensely hateful, and intensely deluded.
Because of his intense passion, he repeatedly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of passion;
because of his intense hatred, he repeatedly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of hatred;
and because of his intense delusion, he repeatedly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of delusion.
For him, these five supramundane faculties become superior, sharp, and swift-acting.
Which five?
Namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

Because these five supramundane faculties are of superior degree and proceed swiftly, he very quickly touches the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*)—that is, for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*).
This is the painful practice with swift direct knowledge.
In that regard, what is the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge?
Here, a certain person is by nature one who has little passion and little hatred.
By having little passion, he does not repeatedly experience the suffering and mental distress born of passion;
by having little hatred, he does not repeatedly experience the suffering and mental distress born of hatred;
by having little delusion, he does not repeatedly experience the suffering and mental distress born of delusion.
For him, these five supramundane faculties are sluggish, weak, not sharp, and not swift-moving.
Which five?
Namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

Because these five faculties are sluggish, weak, and do not proceed rapidly, he touches only a sluggish immediate concentration (ānantarya-samādhi), namely, for the destruction of the outflows (āsrava). This is the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge (sukhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā).
In that regard, what is the pleasant practice with swift higher knowledge?
Here, a certain person is by nature one who has little passion, little hatred, and little delusion.
Because he has little passion, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of passion;
because he has little hatred, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of hatred;
because he has little delusion, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of delusion.
For him, these five supramundane faculties are superior, sharp, and swift-moving.
What are the five?
Namely: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

Because these five faculties are superior, sharp, and swift-moving, he very quickly touches the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*)—that is to say, for the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*). This is called the easy practice with quick direct knowledge.
These, monks, are the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
[12] In that regard, what are the four developments of concentration? ...
There is, monks, a development of concentration which, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision.
There is a development of concentration which, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed, leads to the attainment of wisdom.

In this regard, what is the cultivation of concentration that, when practiced, developed, and cultivated repeatedly, leads to the abandonment of sensual desire? Here, monks, a monk contemplates this very body—above the soles of the feet and below the hair of the head, bounded by skin—as it is situated and as it is disposed, full of various kinds of impurities, with right wisdom and according to reality: namely, that this body has arisen in succession, is subject to unprecedented destruction, is a collection of atoms, is porous, and is a source of oozing from its many openings, such as the nostrils and pores of the skin.
Like an anthill, it is the dwelling place of venomous serpents;
[the body] is produced by those venomous serpents.
It is an enemy of ignorance that commits treachery against both friends and enemies.
Like a bad friend, it is deceptive;
like a mass of foam, it is inherently weak;
like a bubble on water, it arises, breaks, and dissolves.
It is deceptive like a mirage;
it is pithless when peeled away like a plantain tree;
it is of the nature of a trick like an illusion.
Like a king, he disregards commands;
like an enemy, he watches for a downfall;
like a thief, he is not to be trusted.
Like an enemy, he seeks one's harm;
like an executioner, he creates an obstacle to the life of wisdom;
like an empty village, he is devoid of Māra.
Like a potter's vessel, it is open at its mouth; like a bowl of fat, it drips with impurities, being filled with various kinds of filth.
It is as cruel as a serpent that does not move; it possesses a sharp odor like that of a corpse;
and it is a source of impurity like a chamber of excrement.
It speaks like one who cannot endure pain;
it pierces like a thorn;
it is difficult to deal with like a wicked master.
It is to be maintained through repair like an old house;
it is to be carried with repairs like a worn-out boat;
it is to be protected with care like an unbaked clay pot.
Like a wicked friend, it must be constantly guarded;
like a tree on a riverbank, it is unstable and wavering;
and like the current of a great river, it ends in the ocean of death.
It is a dwelling place for all suffering, like a transient inn;
it is unowned, like a shelter for the destitute;
it is to be overcome by stratagem, like the bolt of a thief’s door.
It is constantly beset like a frontier city;
it is prone to collapse like a city of sand;
and it is insatiable like fire.
Like the ocean, it is difficult to fill;
like a basket for all things, it must be protected from falling leaves; like a young child, it must be constantly nurtured.
Like a broken vessel, he must be constantly avoided; like a false deity, he is perpetually possessed by evil; like a vessel containing poison, he must be shunned.
Like borrowed goods for a momentary purpose,
or like a cart for the sake of carrying a load,
it should be borne solely with the intention of dharma.
Furthermore, monks, a monk should examine this body by way of its primary and subsequent causes.
The primary cause of this body here is its origination from the semen and blood of the mother and father;
the subsequent [causes] consist of the quantity of food and so forth.
Food taken in mouthfuls, as soon as it is swallowed, goes to the receptacle of phlegm (*śleṣmāśaya*).
Having reached the receptacle of phlegm, it is liquefied by the phlegm and becomes utterly impure. From the phlegm, it goes to the receptacle of bile (*pittāśaya*).
Having reached the seat of bile (*pittāśaya*), it is digested and becomes hot, then proceeds to the seat of wind (*vāyvāśaya*).
Having been cooked, upon reaching the seat of wind, it is separated by the wind into waste matter (*mala*) and essence (*sāra*), each separately.
From the waste comes impurities such as urine and feces; from the essence, blood is transformed,
and from blood, flesh.
From flesh comes fat; from fat, bones;
from bones, marrow.
From marrow comes semen.

Thus, seeing that this body is impure due to such primary and subsequent causes, the monk perceives this body as raised up by nine hundred and sixty bones, like a house of wretched wood, and bound together by three hundred and fifty sinews.
It is bent by four hundred networks of veins,
smeared with five hundred masses of flesh,
and a conglomeration of many hundreds of veins.
It is bent by seven hundred veins,
bound together by nine hundred sinews, and made lattice-like by the arteries.
It is covered with eighty million and seven hundred thousand joints like a shattered vessel,
with openings for the five sense-faculties,
and seven receptacles (or seven storehouses).
Full of impurity;
with a handful of brain matter, with a handful of fat.
There are three añjali-measures of fat,
six añjali-measures of phlegm,
and six añjali-measures of bile.
The entire [body] has been drawn away by the wind;
[it consists of] one āḍhaka of blood and six prasthas of feces, along with these very same [other elements].
It is filled with distinct, equal [elements],
enveloped by seven layers of skin, and possessed of six tastes.
The bile, entered by the bodily fire and the digestive heat (*agni-hotra*), is constantly agitated; it is difficult to perceive with all the limbs of the body and is foul-smelling by its very nature.
What self-conceit or sense of great pride can there be here?
It should be carried by one with a mind set on Dharma, like borrowed goods for a momentary purpose, or like a cart for the carrying of a load.
Beholding such a body, a mere heap of impurities, one who is proud of their form dwells in arrogance;
for he is of childish intellect, perceiving this world as something real.
The vehicle does not go if it is not conscious.
The body carries away what is pleasant and always carries away what is disagreeable; it is ever being cast off.
Since a living being’s body is so utterly impure, like a worm, how can there be passion for it or any sense of high esteem?
"Contemplating in this way," and so forth.
It is as follows, monks: suppose there were a granary with doors on both sides, full of various kinds of grain, such as rice, sesame, mustard, mung beans, barley, and black lentils.
A man with sight, looking closely at it, would know: "These are awned grains."
"These are fruits and grains.
In the same way, monks, a monk contemplates this very body, however it is positioned and however it is disposed, up to [the full extent of its constituent parts].
This cultivation of concentration, when practiced and frequently cultivated, leads to the abandonment of sensual desire."
In this regard, monks, what is the cultivation of concentration that, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life?

Here, monks, a monk— having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling— moistens, fills, and suffuses this very body internally and personally with a joy and happiness born of seclusion.
He thoroughly gladdens and completely suffuses it; there is no part of his entire body that remains unsuffused or untouched by the joy and happiness born of seclusion within himself.

Just as, monks, blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, or white lotuses, born in the water and submerged in the water, are all drenched, saturated, filled, refreshed, and suffused by cool water; even so, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, drenches, saturates, and [fills] this very body internally and personally with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
It fulfills, pervades, and gladdens; there is no part of his entire body that remains unpermeated or unpervaded by the joy and bliss born of seclusion within—
this cultivation of concentration, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to happiness in the present life.
It conduces to dwelling in peace.

In this regard, monks, what is the cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision? Here, monks, a monk has properly, thoroughly, and well grasped the perception of light; it is well-attended to, well-seen, and firmly established. He cultivates a mind that is equally luminous, sustained by the perception of day, such that at night it is as it was by day.
As it is at night, so it is by day; as it was before, so it is after;
as it is after, so it was before.

"Just as it is below, so it is above; just as it is above, so it is below"— with a mind thus expanded and unconfined, he cultivates a state of mind established in the perception of day, characterized by uniform radiance.

Monks, it is just as, for example, in the last month of summer, on a cloudless day when the sky is free of clouds, at the time of midday, the light becomes perfectly pure, completely cleansed, and radiant;
it does not become so during that time of darkness.

In the same way, monks, when a monk has properly, thoroughly, and well grasped the perception of light—unconfused, well-restrained, and established in the perception of novelty—he cultivates a mind of equal radiance, such that as it is by day, so it is by night; as it is by night, so it is by day;
as it was before, so it is after.
Just as behind, so in front;
just as above, so below; just as below, so above—with an expanded mind, unobstructed, and established in the perception of day, one cultivates a mind of equal radiance.
This cultivation of concentration, when practiced, developed, and frequently cultivated, leads to the attainment of knowledge, vision, and eloquence.
In that regard, what is the cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of wisdom?
Here, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, [contemplates] the pleasure (or pain)...

And because of the abandoning [of these], and because joy and dejection have already vanished beforehand, he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
This cultivation of concentration, when practiced, developed, and cultivated extensively, leads to the attainment of wisdom.
These are the four cultivations of meditative concentration.
[13] In this regard, monks, what are the four foundations of mindfulness?

Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the body in the external body...

He dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in internal feelings, in external feelings, and in both internal and external feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

He dwells contemplating the mind in the internal mind, in the external mind, and in both internal and external minds, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

One dwells contemplating phenomena in internal phenomena, in external phenomena, and in both internal and external phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world;
these are the four foundations of mindfulness.
[14] In this regard, monks, what are the four right efforts?
Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, and strives for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen.
He exerts vigor,
restrains the mind,
and applies himself correctly.
He generates desire, exerts himself, and arouses energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states that have already arisen.
He uplifts the mind and applies it correctly;
he generates desire for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen.
He exerts himself, arouses energy,
and uplifts the mind.
He applies himself correctly.
For the stability, cultivation, non-confusion, non-decline, further increase, growth, expansion, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen, he generates desire, exerts effort, and strives.
One arouses energy,
upholds the mind, and correctly applies it;
these are the four right efforts.

[15] In this regard, what are the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)? Here, monks, a monk cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the concentration of desire and the formative forces of abandonment; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment. This... [ensures that] his energy will be neither slack nor over-exerted. (2)

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and the formative forces of abandonment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, [thinking]: "May my mind not become overly slack, nor too exerted. (3)

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and concentration through investigation, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, [thinking]: "May my investigation be neither too slack nor too tense. 4.
Monks, these are the four bases of psychic power.
[16] In this regard, monks, what are the five faculties?
Namely: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Among these, what is the faculty of faith?
By means of which faith one has faith in four things.
Which four? One maintains the mundane right view pertaining to the realm of saṃsāra.
He becomes one who relies upon the ripening of karma,
thinking: "Whatever action I shall perform, whether wholesome or unwholesome, I shall experience the ripening of that very action."
Even for the sake of his life, he does not perform an evil deed;
this is called the faculty of faith.
In that regard, what is the faculty of energy?
Those phenomena which one has faith in through the faculty of faith,
those very phenomena one brings to fulfillment through the faculty of energy.
This is called the faculty of energy.
In that regard, what is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?
Those phenomena which one brings to fulfillment by means of the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*), those very phenomena one [maintains] by means of the faculty of mindfulness... ||
...it causes them not to be lost.
This is called the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya).
In that regard, what is the faculty of wisdom?
Those phenomena which one makes one-pointed by means of the faculty of concentration,
those very phenomena one penetrates by means of the faculty of wisdom.
He becomes one whose nature is to investigate those phenomena;
this is called the faculty of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five faculties.
[17] In this regard, monks, what are the five powers?
Namely: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
And these are called "powers" because they cannot be crushed by the afflictions, which act like servants.
These, monks, are the five powers.
[18] In this regard, monks, what are the seven factors of enlightenment? Namely:

the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment that is energy, the factor of enlightenment that is rapture, the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, the factor of enlightenment that is concentration, and the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity.
In this regard, monks, a monk cultivates the factor of awakening that is mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
In this way, he cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is vigor, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is joy, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
These, monks, are the seven factors of enlightenment.
[19] In this regard, monks, what is the Noble Eightfold Path?
It is as follows: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This, monks, is called the Noble Eightfold Path.
In that regard, what is right view?

It is that which is supramundane; it does not arise from the view of a self, nor from [the views of] a being, a soul, a life-principle, a person, a human, or a man; it does not arise from the views of annihilationism or eternalism, nor from the views of existence or non-existence, nor from views that are wholesome or indeterminate.
And that which does not arise from the views of cyclic existence or nirvana—
this is called right view.
In that regard, what is right resolve? It is that one does not form those resolves by which the afflictions of passion, hatred, and delusion arise.
He forms those intentions by which the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision and knowledge of liberation arise;
this is called right intention.
In that regard, what is right speech?
It is that by which one does not torment oneself or others through passion,
nor does one afflict oneself or others.
He does not harm himself or others;
he is endowed with that speech which is composed and disciplined,
by means of which he correctly instructs and exhorts.
This is called right speech.
In that regard, what is right action?
It is that one does not perform any action which is black and has a black ripening.
He does not perform that karma which is black-and-white with black-and-white ripening;
he does not perform that karma which has black-and-white ripening, nor that which is entirely black...
it conduces to the exhaustion of karma; he performs that karma.
One performs wholesome actions;
one whose sphere of activity has wholesome actions as its refuge—
this is called right action.

In that regard, what is right livelihood? It is the state of relinquishing for the sake of one's purpose through the refinement of virtues; it is the absence of hypocrisy, the absence of flattery, the absence of extortion, the absence of seeking gain through gain, and the absence of longing for future worlds.
Contentment with one's own person and one's lot, freedom from blemish, and a livelihood known by the noble ones—
this is called right livelihood.
In that regard, what is right effort? It is that effort which is false, which is underlain by the latent tendencies of the afflictions— ignorance, attachment, aversion, and delusion.
He does not desire that exertion;
rather, he pursues that exertion which correctly enters the truth of the Noble Path and provides the practice leading to Nirvana.
This is called right effort.
In that regard, what is right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*)?

It is that mindfulness which is well-established, unshakable, straight, and not crooked; which perceives the faults and dangers of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and leads one along the path to nirvāṇa; it is a pervasive awareness and the non-forgetting of the noble path. This is called right mindfulness.
In that regard, what is right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)?
It is the concentration that is characterized by correctness.
Abiding in which concentration, for the sake of the liberation of all sentient beings, one enters into the state of being correctly established in the path of certainty (*niyāma*).
This is called right concentration;
this is called the noble eightfold path.
[20] In this regard, monks, what is mindfulness of breathing in its sixteen aspects?
Breathing in short or long, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing in."
Breathing out long, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out long. Breathing in short, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in short.
Or, breathing out short, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out short."

Experiencing the body while breathing in, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing in experiencing the body. Experiencing the body while breathing out, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing out experiencing the body.
Experiencing the bodily formations while breathing in, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing in experiencing the bodily formations."
Experiencing the bodily formations while inhaling, or experiencing the bodily formations while exhaling, one understands it as it truly is.
Experiencing the whole body while inhaling, one understands as it truly is: "I am experiencing the whole body while inhaling.
Experiencing the bodily formations while inhaling, or not experiencing the bodily formations while exhaling, one understands it as it truly is.

Breathing in while experiencing the whole body, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in while experiencing the whole body. Breathing out while experiencing the whole body, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out while experiencing the whole body. Breathing in while experiencing the bodily formations, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in while experiencing the bodily formations"; breathing out while experiencing the bodily formations... [he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out while experiencing the bodily formations"].
He understands, as it truly is, "I am breathing out while experiencing [the breath].
He understands, as it truly is, "Calming my bodily formations, I am breathing in; calming my bodily formations, I am breathing in.
He understands, as it truly is, "Calming my bodily formations, I am breathing out; calming my bodily formations, I am breathing out."

Experiencing joy while inhaling, he understands as it really is: "I am inhaling while experiencing joy. Experiencing joy while exhaling, he understands as it really is: "I am exhaling while experiencing joy."

Experiencing pleasure while breathing in, one knows as it really is: "I am breathing in experiencing pleasure. Experiencing pleasure while breathing out, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing out experiencing pleasure. Experiencing the mind while breathing in, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing in experiencing the mind."

Experiencing the mind while breathing out, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out experiencing the mind. Experiencing the mental formations while breathing in, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in experiencing the mental formations."

Experiencing the mental formations while breathing out, he understands as it really is: "Experiencing the mental formations, I am breathing out. Calming the mental formations while breathing in, he understands as it really is: "Calming the mental formations, I am breathing in."
Experiencing the calming of the mental formations while breathing out, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out, experiencing the calming of the mental formations.
Experiencing joy in his mind while breathing in, he understands as it really is: "My mind is experiencing joy as I breathe in.
Experiencing joy in his mind while breathing out, he understands as it really is: "My mind is experiencing joy as I breathe out."
Breathing in while his mind is being liberated, he understands as it really is: "My mind is being liberated; I am breathing in while my mind is being liberated.
Breathing out while his mind is being liberated, he understands as it really is: "My mind is being liberated; I am breathing out while my mind is being liberated."
Breathing in with a concentrated mind, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in with a concentrated mind.
Breathing out with a concentrated mind, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out with a concentrated mind.

Likewise, observing impermanence, observing dispassion, observing cessation, and observing relinquishment, while breathing in and observing relinquishment, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in observing relinquishment."
Or, observing relinquishment while breathing out, he understands as it really is: "Observing relinquishment, I am breathing out.
Monks, this is the sixteen-fold mindfulness of breathing.

[21] In that regard, what are the four factors of stream-entry? Here, monks, a disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, thinking: "Thus indeed is the Blessed One: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."

He is endowed with verified clarity regarding the Dharma: "The Dharma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized individually by the wise, namely:

the subduing of pride and intoxication, the removal of the underlying tendencies, the uprooting of the storehouse-consciousness, the cutting off of the flow of phenomena, the non-apprehension of emptiness, the exhaustion of craving, cessation, and Nirvana."

He is endowed with verified confidence in the Saṅgha: "The noble Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well, practicing rightly, practicing correctly, practicing appropriately, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, and living according to the Dharma;
in the Saṅgha there are those who have entered the path for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry;
in the Saṅgha there are stream-enterers."
In the Saṅgha there are those who have entered the path for the realization of the fruit of once-returning;
in the Saṅgha there are once-returners;
in the Saṅgha there are those who have entered the path for the realization of the fruit of non-returning.
In the Saṅgha there are non-returners;
in the Saṅgha there are those practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship;
in the Saṅgha there are arhats.
Namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals.

This is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, endowed with faith, endowed with learning, endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation.

He is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of salutation with joined palms, worthy of respectful treatment, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world, and beautiful to behold— namely, because he is endowed with the virtues beloved by the noble ones, which are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, faultless, liberating, unadulterated, well-integrated, praised by the wise, leading to victory, and not censured by the wise. These are the four factors of stream-entry.
[22] Monks, what are the ten powers of a Tathāgata?
A Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the possible as possible, and he understands, as it truly is, the impossible as impossible.
This is the first power of a Tathāgata:
he understands, as it truly is, the ripening of the undertaking of karmic actions in the past, future, and present;
and he understands, as it truly is, the ripening of the various inclinations of other beings and other individuals.

He understands, as it truly is, that among the worlds of many world-systems, there are worlds of diverse elements. He understands, as it truly is, the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other beings.
He understands, as it truly is, the path leading everywhere, which leads to various destinations.

He understands, as they truly are, the defilements and purifications regarding the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments of other beings. He recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes, details, and specific characteristics;
he recollects even a single birth.
"He recollects two, three, four, and even many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of births," and so forth.
With the divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn;
he sees them being born in happy or miserable destinies according to their good or bad conduct of body, speech, and mind, and so forth.
Through the destruction of the outflows, he understands, by means of wisdom, the untainted liberation of mind as it truly is.
These, monks, are the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
[23] What, monks, are the four grounds of self-confidence of the Tathāgata?
Herein, the Blessed One, being perfectly enlightened, knows himself thus:

"Regarding these dharmas that have not been fully realized by you, no one in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, including gods and humans, could raise a valid objection."
He perceives this sign thoroughly.
Perceiving the sign, the Tathāgata, the Blessed One—having attained security and having attained fearlessness—recognizes his place as the leader of the herd;
having entered the assembly correctly, he roars the lion’s roar.
He sets in motion the Brahma-wheel, which has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding those things declared by the Tathāgatas to be obstructive factors, for one who indulges in them, no one could rightfully bring a charge that they do not constitute an obstruction; such is the detailed explanation.
Or, regarding that noble path declared by him as leading to liberation— which, if one were to disparage it as inferior,
would not lead to the complete destruction of suffering for anyone else— herein [the argument] is as before.

When one who has exhausted the outflows (āsrava) declares himself to be such, if anyone in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation of recluses and brahmins, including gods and humans, were to bring forth a challenge, saying, "These outflows have not been fully exhausted," the Tathāgata perceives no ground for such a claim.
Seeing no such ground, the Tathāgata dwells having attained confidence and having attained fearlessness. He says: [I am the Lion’s Roar].
He knows the ground;
having entered the assembly rightly, he roars the lion’s roar and turns the Brahma-wheel, which has not been turned by any ascetic, brahmin, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma.
Monks, these are the four grounds of self-confidence of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata.
[24] What are the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the Tathāgata?

Namely: the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
These, monks, are the four analytical knowledges.
[25] Monks, what are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
The Tathāgata has no physical lapse, and he has no vocal outcry.
There is no loss of mindfulness, there is no unconcentrated mind,
and there is no perception of diversity.
There is no equanimity that is not preceded by discernment; there is no loss of aspiration;
there is no loss of vigor.
There is no loss of mindfulness, no loss of wisdom,
and no loss of liberation.
The three knowledges and visions of liberation:
unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past time,
and unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the future time.
In the present time, there is unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision;
all bodily action is preceded by knowledge and is followed by the transformation of perception; all vocal action is preceded by knowledge and is followed by knowledge.
All his mental actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge.
These, monks, are the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata.
[26] In that regard, what are the thirty-two marks of a great person (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata?
The Tathāgata has well-placed feet; this is a mark of a great person.
On the soles of his feet, there are wheels marked with a thousand spokes.
He has long heels and well-proportioned feet;
he has long fingers;
and his hands and feet are webbed.
Soft and youthful hands and feet; a body with seven prominent elevations; shanks like those of the eneya antelope.
The private organ is concealed within a sheath;
the upper body is like that of a lion;
and the space between the shoulders is well-filled.
Well-restrained shoulders; lack of protuberance;
and long-reaching arms.
Purity of the eyes;
a neck like a conch shell; and a jaw like that of a lion.
He has forty even teeth;
his teeth are even and without gaps;
his teeth are brilliantly white.
The tongue is long and slender; it possesses the excellence of perceiving the finest flavors;
and its voice is like the Brahma-voice and the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
The quality of having deep blue eyes; the quality of having eyelashes like those of a cow; and the quality of having delicate skin.
A skin of golden color;
each hair grows from a single pore;
and the body hairs grow upward and curl to the right.
Hair as dark blue as sapphire;
a tuft of hair (ūrṇā) between the eyebrows that is very white and located on the forehead;
and a protuberance on the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa).
The symmetry of a banyan tree and universal loveliness; the strength of Mahānārāyaṇa and universal loveliness—
this is a mark of a great person belonging to the Tathāgata, the Great Person.
These, monks, are the marks of a Great Man belonging to the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s feet are well-placed; this mark of a great person (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) was produced in the past through his firmness in undertaking commitments. On the soles of his feet there are wheels with a thousand spokes; this mark of a great person was produced in the past through his not acting deceptively toward other beings. His heels are long and his feet are well-knit; this mark of a great person was produced in the past through his honoring his parents and serving at their feet.

The Tathāgata’s mark of a great person consisting of long fingers was produced in the past by providing protection, shelter, and defense for the Dharma. The Tathāgata’s mark of a great person consisting of webbed hands and feet was produced in the past by not causing division among retinues.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great person consisting of soft and tender hands and feet was produced in the past by giving various types of clothing and food.
The quality of having a body with seven protuberances: this mark of a Great Man of the Tathāgata was produced by his being well-disposed toward the service of others.

... The quality of having pure eyes: this mark of a Great Man of the Tathāgata was produced by his former diligent undertaking of the ten paths of wholesome action. The quality of having a neck like a conch shell: this mark of a Great Man of the Tathāgata was produced by his former giving of various medicines and food to the sick.

The lion-like jaw: this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced by his former application of roots of merit. The possession of forty even teeth: this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced by his former application of providing consolation to sentient beings.
The possession of teeth without gaps: this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced by his former act of reuniting the divided masses of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great person, even-teeth, was produced in the past by his gift of pleasing jewels.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great person, very white teeth, was produced in the past by his well-guarded conduct of body, speech, and mind. [The mark of] abundant (thin) teeth...
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of a broad tongue was produced in the past through speaking the truth.

The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of having the most excellent sense of taste was produced in the past by having accumulated immeasurable masses of merit and by being supremely devoted to selflessness.

The Tathāgata’s possession of a voice like that of Brahmā or the kalaviṅka bird is a mark of a Great Man; it was produced in the past by his speaking kindly to sentient beings and by his causing them to hear words of joy.
The Tathāgata’s possession of deep blue eyes is a mark of a Great Man; it was produced in the past by his protecting sentient beings with loving-kindness.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great person, having eyelashes like those of a cow, was produced in the past through natural purity.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great person, having delicate skin, was produced in the past through the flexibility of mind in protecting the harmony of the Dharma.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, which is having skin the color of gold, was produced in the past by his giving of pleasant bedding, seats, and coverings, as well as agreeable speech.

The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, which is having a single hair per pore, was produced in the past by his avoidance of social crowds. The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, which is having body hairs that curl to the right, was produced in the past by his receiving the instructions of teachers, preceptors, and spiritual friends with respectful compliance.

The quality of having hair as dark blue as sapphire: this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced in the past through compassion for all living beings and by refraining from using clods of earth, sticks, or weapons.

The quality of having a white ūrṇā-hair between the eyebrows on a beautiful forehead: this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced in the past through speaking in praise of those worthy of praise.

The quality of having a protuberance on the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa): this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced in the past through showing reverence and bowing before one’s teachers.

The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, which is the symmetrical proportion of a banyan tree and universal loveliness, was brought about in the past by his application of himself and other beings to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, which is the universal loveliness of his body, was brought about in the past by his making images of the Tathāgata and by his restoring ruined stūpas for others.
And it is produced through the consolation and unification of those who are afraid;
and because the Tathāgata possesses mastery over those dharmas by means of immeasurable roots of virtue, the thirty-two marks of a great man are produced upon his body.

[27] What are the eighty secondary marks? The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have copper-colored nails; they have glossy nails; they have prominent nails; they have rounded fingernails; they have well-proportioned fingers; they have tapering fingers; they have hidden veins; they have veins free from knots; they have hidden ankles; and they have a gait with the stride of a lion.

They walk with the stride of an elephant, they walk with the stride of a swan, and they walk with the stride of a bull; they walk turning to the right, they walk gracefully, their limbs are straight, their limbs are rounded, their limbs are well-proportioned, their bodies are broad and majestic, their secondary marks are complete, their gait is even, their limbs are pure, their limbs are soft, their limbs are purified, their limbs are prominent, their limbs are well-knit, and their minor members are well-distributed.

They have eyes pure and free from darkness; their bellies are rounded, smooth, and unmarred; they have slender waists and deep navels that curl to the right; they are serene and pleasing on all sides; their conduct is pure; their bodies are free of moles or blemishes; their hands are as soft and delicate as cotton-wool; the lines on their palms are glossy, deep, and complete; and their faces are small and well-proportioned.

They have faces with teeth like the reflection of a mirror-image; they have soft tongues, copper-colored tongues, and voices like the roar of an elephant or the thunder of clouds; they have sweet, deep, and charming voices; they have rounded fangs, sharp and even fangs, and well-proportioned fangs;

they have prominent noses, clean noses, wide eyes, long eyelashes, eyes like blooming lotuses, eyes like the petals of a blue lotus, broad and full eyes, long eyebrows, eyebrows with even hairs, glossy eyebrows, thick and long ears, and symmetrical ears.

The Blessed Buddhas have unimpaired ears, well-rounded foreheads, perfectly full [facial features], hair resembling bees, circular hair, white hair, untangled hair, non-rough hair, and beautiful hair;
their soles bear the marks of the śrīvatsa, the svastika, the nandyāvarta, the wheel, the vajra, the lotus, the fish, and so forth.
Monks, these are the eighty secondary marks manifested upon the body of the Tathāgata.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, I shall teach you the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end;

I shall reveal the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and pristine—namely, the Dharma-discourse called 'The Determination of Meaning' (*Arthaviniścaya*). Since this was said, this [present work] is the response thereto.

"Monks, dwell in forest retreats, empty huts, mountain clefts, mountain caves, heaps of straw, open spaces under the sky, cemeteries, and forest thickets... Monks, do not be negligent; lest you later come to regret it.
This is my instruction."
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the minds of five hundred bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks and that entire assembly—including the world of gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas—rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.
The Dharma discourse titled "The Noble Determination of Meanings" is completed.
